goal: See linear algebra as the study of consistent ways to move space: vectors are moves, bases are measuring sticks, matrices record basis images, and determinants and eigenvectors expose what a transformation preserves.

lessons.objective: By the end you can recognize a linear transformation in a moving grid and predict which features stay coherent.

beats.text: Watch a square grid stretch, shear, and flatten while the origin stays pinned. Ask: what single rule could move every point so coherently?
Compare a translation, a bend, and a grid shear. Which one preserves the origin and keeps every straight line straight?
Track a point as a weighted combination of two arrows, then move the arrows and the point by the same rule.
Linearity means T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v), T(cu)=cT(u), and T(0)=0: combinations survive the move.
Stretching, rotating, shearing, and flattening are different faces of one idea: a consistent map of vector space.
Say the test aloud: origin fixed, sums preserved, scalings preserved. A linear map preserves the grid's combination structure.

visuals.title: The plane as a rubber grid
visuals.goal: Make a coherent grid deformation and the fixed origin immediately visible.

visuals.title: Move the grid yourself
visuals.goal: Let the learner test stretch, shear, rotation, and flattening with four matrix entries.

lessons.objective: By the end you can add and scale vectors as reusable displacements and distinguish an arrow's location from its move.

beats.text: Slide the same arrow to three places. The scenery changes, but the instruction ‘move right two and up one’ does not.
If two arrows have equal length and direction but different tails, are they different vectors or copies of one move?
Place one arrow head-to-tail after another and draw the shortcut from the first tail to the last head.
A vector is a displacement; componentwise addition combines moves and scalar multiplication changes their amount or reverses them.
Vectors give linear algebra its movable pieces: every later transformation acts on these reusable instructions.
Name the three operations: translate the arrow without changing it, add displacements componentwise, and scale every component together.

visuals.title: Arrows are moves
visuals.goal: Separate a vector's displacement from the location of its drawn arrow.

visuals.title: Vectors through a map
visuals.goal: Compare input vectors with their transformed arrows on the same grid.

lessons.objective: By the end you can use two independent vectors as a basis and read a vector's coordinates as coefficients of those moves.

beats.text: Replace the familiar horizontal and vertical arrows with two oblique arrows. Can every point still be reached by taking enough of each?
What goes wrong if the two proposed basis arrows lie on one line? Which points become unreachable?
Take a copies of the first arrow and b copies of the second, then add them to land on a chosen target.
A basis spans the plane and is independent: every vector has one and only one coordinate recipe in that basis.
Coordinates are not labels glued to a vector; they are instructions relative to selected measuring directions.
Check a basis by asking two questions: can its arrows reach every vector, and is the recipe unique?

visuals.title: Two moves span a plane
visuals.goal: Show oblique basis vectors generating a complete parallelogram lattice.

visuals.title: The matrix as a new grid
visuals.goal: Connect basis vectors to the two visible columns and their generated lattice.

lessons.objective: By the end you can test a rule for additivity and homogeneity and explain why those two properties control every linear combination.

beats.text: Send u and v through a mysterious machine. The machine either respects the shortcut u+v or breaks it; watch for the moment the two paths disagree.
Does preserving straightness alone guarantee a linear map? Test a translation and a curved rule against the origin and sums.
Split a vector into a weighted sum of basis arrows, transform each ingredient, and recombine the outputs.
T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v) follows from additivity and homogeneity, so two basis images determine the entire map.
Linearity is a promise about combinations, not about preserving sizes: the map may rotate, stretch, shear, or collapse.
A rule earns the word linear when it respects both addition and scalar multiplication, including the forced fixed origin.

visuals.title: Combinations survive
visuals.goal: Make the split-transform-recombine path coincide with transforming the sum directly.

visuals.title: Linearity laboratory
visuals.goal: Experiment with maps whose transformed grid preserves combinations.

lessons.objective: By the end you can construct a matrix from the images of a basis and use its columns to calculate a transformed vector.

beats.text: A whole grid moves, yet two arrows seem to control everything. Which two arrows would you measure first?
If the input is (x,y), why should x multiply one visible arrow while y multiplies the other?
Transform i and j, place their outputs as columns, and assemble xT(i)+yT(j) for a sample input.
The matrix [T(i) T(j)] stores the map in its columns, so matrix-vector multiplication is exactly linear recombination.
A matrix is not just a rectangle of numbers; it is a map's coordinate portrait relative to chosen bases.
To build a standard-basis matrix, transform the first unit vector for column one and the second for column two.

visuals.title: Read the columns as arrows
visuals.goal: Tie each matrix column to one transformed basis vector and a transformed grid edge.

visuals.title: Where does the unit square go?
visuals.goal: Let the learner change a, b, c, and d while seeing the two column arrows move.

lessons.objective: By the end you can compose two linear maps in the correct order and explain why the corresponding matrices multiply in that order.

beats.text: Pass the same grid through a stretch and a shear. Swapping the machines changes the final picture; why does order matter?
In AB, which map sees the original vector first, A or B? Trace one arrow through both labels before calculating.
Transform each column of B with A, then place those two outputs as the columns of the composite map.
ABv=A(Bv): the rightmost factor acts first, and matrix multiplication combines row dot columns to encode that chain.
Composition turns transformations into a language for building complex motion from simple stages.
Read a product right to left, apply each map to the current vector, and expect AB and BA to differ unless the maps commute.

visuals.title: Two machines in a row
visuals.goal: Make right-to-left matrix order and noncommutativity visible on one grid.

visuals.title: Stack the maps
visuals.goal: Compare the matrix columns and area after changing the four entries.

lessons.objective: By the end you can compute a 2×2 determinant and interpret its magnitude as area scaling and its sign as orientation.

beats.text: Fill a unit square with glowing ink, transform it, and watch one number track the signed area of the new parallelogram.
What should the area number say after a reflection, a double stretch, or a flattening onto one line?
Use the two matrix columns as edge vectors and compare the parallelogram area with ad−bc.
det(A)=ad−bc: absolute value is the area multiplier, while the sign records whether orientation was preserved or reversed.
The determinant compresses a two-dimensional geometric story into one scalar without forgetting collapse or handedness.
Read det as signed area scale. Zero means the plane has lost a dimension and the map cannot be one-to-one.

visuals.title: Area has a sign
visuals.goal: Connect ad−bc to the oriented area of the transformed unit square.

visuals.title: Tune the area
visuals.goal: Let the learner drive the determinant toward positive, negative, and zero values.

lessons.objective: By the end you can decide when a 2×2 map is invertible and explain an inverse as a transformation that restores lost coordinates.

beats.text: Run a grid forward through A and try to rewind it. A reversible parallelogram returns home; a flattened sheet cannot remember where points came from.
What information disappears when det(A)=0, and why would no second rule be able to recover it?
Swap the diagonal entries, negate the off-diagonals, divide by the determinant, and test the product against the identity.
A⁻¹=(1/(ad−bc))[[d,−b],[−c,a]] for nonzero determinant; AA⁻¹=I means every vector is restored.
Invertibility is information preservation: a map can distort a grid dramatically and still be reversible if it never collapses a direction.
Check det first. Nonzero gives a unique undo map; zero signals multiple inputs share an output and no inverse exists.

visuals.title: Forward and backward
visuals.goal: Show the inverse as a real undoing process and isolate collapse as the obstruction.

visuals.title: Find a reversible map
visuals.goal: Use the determinant display to distinguish recoverable and collapsed grids.

lessons.objective: By the end you can identify an eigenvector direction and interpret its eigenvalue as the signed scale factor along that direction.

beats.text: Sweep a fan of arrows through a shear. Almost every arrow turns, but one line keeps its heading while its length changes.
Is a vector an eigenvector because it stays at the same point, or because its output lies on the same line?
Set Av=λv, rearrange to (A−λI)v=0, and demand a nonzero solution by setting the determinant to zero.
Eigenvectors are invariant directions and λ records stretch, shrink, or reversal; a rotation can have no real invariant direction.
Eigenvectors reveal the axes a transformation naturally prefers, even when the standard coordinate grid hides them.
Look for Av parallel to v, not Av equal to v. The scalar relating them is the eigenvalue, and v must be nonzero.

visuals.title: The directions that survive
visuals.goal: Highlight invariant lines and distinguish fixed vectors from scaled eigenvectors.

visuals.title: Hunt eigen-directions
visuals.goal: Show real eigenvalue lines while the matrix sliders change the map.

lessons.objective: By the end you can convert coordinates between bases and explain why the same geometric map gets a different matrix in a different coordinate system.

beats.text: Keep one arrow frozen while two coordinate grids rotate beneath it. The arrow has not moved, yet its coordinate pair changes.
Which object changed: the vector, the basis, or the numbers used to describe the vector?
Treat the new basis vectors as columns of P, solve P[new coordinates]=[old geometric vector], and use P⁻¹ to convert back.
Coordinates are representations. With the same basis on both sides, the new matrix is P⁻¹AP: one map seen through a new measuring grid.
Changing basis can turn a hard-looking transformation into a simple one by choosing axes aligned with its natural behavior.
Name the direction of conversion, build the basis matrix from its columns, and apply the correct matrix or inverse in that order.

visuals.title: One arrow, new coordinates
visuals.goal: Keep geometry fixed while coordinate labels change with the basis.

visuals.title: Choose your measuring sticks
visuals.goal: Connect basis columns, inverse conversion, and matrix representation.
